cards.rationale: Exact preimage/candidate hashes match READY; the live row equals the preimage. Utrecht’s Babylonian calendar introduction says the twelve lunar months began at sunset on the first observed or computed crescent after astronomical new moon, supporting the prompt and explanation. NASA supports the full-Moon timing and waning-crescent distractor; USNO supports the equinox note. The four options are distinct celestial/calendar cues, and medium is appropriate for the source-specific Babylonian practice. The related sundial/water-clock cards 042–043 have distinct artifact prompts; this row’s notes name only generic instrument facts and do not identify either artifact.

Exact hashes match READY and live baseline. Hammurabi’s letter to Sin-idinnam explicitly orders the new month registered as a second Elul and shifts tribute to its 25th day, so the added month and explanation are accurate. The Canopus decree’s indexed text supports the sixth epagomenal day each fourth year; Suetonius says Augustus called Sextilis by his name rather than September; UCL supports the Egyptian 365-day calendar and five epagomenal days; Utrecht supports later 7-in-19-year intercalation. Options are comparable calendar changes and medium fits the specific inference. Generic clock notes shared with 042–043 do not disclose the artifact mechanisms.

Exact hashes match READY and live baseline. Gaius I.98–99 defines adrogation as adoption of an independent person, and I.107 says both that person and children formerly under his power fall under the adrogator, with the children assuming the status of grandchildren. The key alieni iuris and explanation are accurate. Each note is supported by Gaius: paternal power, emancipation, agnatic and cognatic kinship; the distractors are plausible Roman legal/family categories. Hard suits the multi-step application. Related Roman-law cards test different rules and the note does not supply their particular keys.

Exact hashes match READY and live baseline. Pliny 10.6 says Roman citizenship had already been granted to Harpocras; Trajan 10.7 explicitly distinguishes that from the later request for Alexandrian citizenship and asks for the Egyptian nome. The prompt, key and explanation preserve this chronology. Gaius supports the Latin-right notes; Pliny 10.94 supports the ius trium liberorum note. The four choices are related civic rights/statuses, and hard is appropriate for the letter sequence. The Harpocras fact is distinct from nearby Roman family-status and peregrine-parentage questions.

Exact hashes match READY and live baseline. Gaius I.76–78 states that where a Roman woman and alien lack connubium, the child is an alien under the lex Minicia; this supports the key and explanation. Gaius I.67 supports the mistaken-status remedy note, I.22–25 supports the freedman distractor notes, and I.55–56 supports the legitimate-marriage/paternal-power note. The fact-specific legal scenario merits hard. Related cards ask about Roman citizenship or family power but do not give this Minician-law case.

Exact hashes match READY and live baseline. The Met identifies the gold octodrachm as Ptolemaic Period and describes Arsinoe II, her veil and stephane, double cornucopia and the legend Arsinoe Philadelphos. This supports the prompt, key and explanation. The Met, Museums Victoria and Berlin collection records support the coin notes for Seleucus I, Antigonus II and the Attalid coin; the four answer options are comparable Hellenistic states. Hard is appropriate for the detailed numismatic identification. The repeated state-note pool in the neighboring Seleucid row describes distinct ruler/coin facts; it does not state that Arsinoe’s coin is Ptolemaic.

Exact hashes match READY and live baseline. The cylinder’s translated text identifies Antiochus as great king, son of Seleucus, and says he laid the foundation of Ezida, Nabû’s temple at Borsippa. The page identifies Antiochus as Seleucid, supporting the key and explanation. The Met, Museums Victoria and Berlin records support the three coin distractor notes; all four options are comparable Hellenistic states. Hard fits the identification from a specific inscription. The neighboring Ptolemaic and other state cards repeat a common answer pool, but no note maps this cylinder’s Antiochus to the Seleucid option, so the catalog does not supply the tested connection.

catalogDependencies.rationale: The prompt concerns Babylonian month starts; notes describe generic sundial and water-clock functions only. They do not reveal the Delos double-hemisphere sundial or the Vitruvian Ctesibius water-clock mechanism.
The clock notes are generic device facts, while 042–043 ask for separate archaeological/mechanical clues; the sibling lunar-month question does not state this Hammurabi letter’s second-Elul case.

Adrogation of an independent father and descendants is distinct from emancipation after repeated mancipation, Pliny’s grant chronology, and the lex Minicia’s child-status rule. The notes do not name the other questions’ tested particulars.
Pliny’s Roman-then-Alexandrian citizenship sequence is separate from family power, kinship, manumission and Minician parentage rules.
The lex Minicia case is unique. Generic notes on citizenship and patria potestas do not establish the status rule for a Roman woman’s child by an alien without connubium.

The Cleopatra card tests co-rule with Caesarion, while this item tests the Met’s Arsinoe II coin attribution. Existing cards about other Hellenistic states and the sibling Seleucid card share a category pool but do not disclose the Arsinoe coin’s issuer/state connection.

These questions reuse the Hellenistic-state answer pool and notes, but none identifies the Antiochus cylinder with a state. The cylinder text itself supplies the Antiochus/Seleucus relation, which is necessary to solve this prompt.
